A Priori Monte Carlo Simulation for Sample Size Planning for RMSEA in SEM

Source: R/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.R
ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.Rd

Conduct a priori Monte Carlo simulation to empirically study the effects of (mis)specifications of input information on the calculated sample size. The sample size is planned so that the expected width of a confidence interval for the population RMSEA is no larger than desired. Random data are generated from the true covariance matrix but fit to the proposed model, whereas the sample size is calculated based on the input covariance matrix and proposed model.

Usage

ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(
  width,
  model,
  true_cov_matrix,
  specified_N = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.9,
  G = 200,
  filename = NULL,
  ...,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

width

desired confidence interval width for the population RMSEA.

model

the model the researcher proposes, which may or may not be the true model, written in lavaan model syntax (see model.syntax). The observed variable names in the model must match the row and column names of true_cov_matrix.

true_cov_matrix

the true population covariance matrix, which is used to generate random data for the simulation study. The row and column names of true_cov_matrix must match the observed variables in model.

specified_N

the total sample size N. If specified_N is given, random samples of that size are generated. Otherwise the sample size is calculated with the sample size planning method so that the expected width of a confidence interval for the population RMSEA is no larger than width, for the interval formed as lavaan forms it (see Details).

conf_level

confidence level of the planned and the simulated intervals (i.e., 1 - the Type I error rate). The default, 0.90, is the conventional level of the RMSEA interval and the default of ss_aipe_rmsea and ci_rmsea.

G

number of replications in the Monte Carlo simulation.

filename

an optional path for a comma separated file recording every converged replication (its index, the RMSEA estimate, the two confidence limits, and the interval width): nothing is written when filename is NULL (the default), a new file with a header row is created otherwise, an existing file at that path is appended to, and a throwaway run should point it at tempfile(fileext = ".csv").

...

additional arguments passed to sem when fitting the model (for example estimator or missing). Every name given here must be an argument or an option of lavaan (see lavOptions); any other name, and any argument without a name, is refused before a model is fitted, with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid that gives the name as it was typed

seed

NULL (the default) to draw from the current random number stream, or a single number that makes the call reproducible; a supplied seed is set for this call only, and the caller's random number state is restored when the function returns.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value summarizing the a priori Monte Carlo study. The term entries are: "mean_rmsea", "median_rmsea", "sd_rmsea" (summaries of the realized RMSEA estimates across the converged replications); "mean_ci_width", "median_ci_width", "sd_ci_width" (summaries of the realized interval widths); "pct_ci_less_width" (proportion of intervals narrower than the target width); "pct_ci_miss_low" and "pct_ci_miss_high" (tail-specific empirical non-coverage of the population RMSEA); "total_type_I_error" (overall empirical non-coverage, the sum of the two tails); and the echoes "total_N" (the N evaluated), "df" (model degrees of freedom), "true_rmsea" (the population RMSEA recovered from fitting model to true_cov_matrix), "width", and "conf_level". The proportion rows are on the 0 to 1 scale, not percentages. The number of converged replications is attr(x, "simulation")$returned (see the section on the record of the simulation).

Details

This function implements the sample size planning method proposed in Kelley and Lai (2011). It uses sem to fit the proposed model to the population covariance matrix, which recovers the population RMSEA (the model misspecification) and the model degrees of freedom, and to fit the model to each simulated sample, and it forms the confidence interval for the population RMSEA in each replication from that sample's chi square statistic, inverted with ci_nc_chisq as sem_fit_measures inverts it. The model is specified in lavaan syntax, so lavaan must be installed.

The population RMSEA is read from lavaan::fitMeasures(), which is computed reliably for the large-sample population fit.

Each replication's interval is formed from the statistic \(T\) of that replication's fit and the sample size multiplier \(a\) lavaan formed \(T\) with (sample_size_convention in ci_rmsea): \(a = N\) for maximum likelihood under lavaan's default normal likelihood, and \(a = N - 1\) under likelihood = "wishart" and for the least squares estimators, either of which ... can request. That is the interval lavaan itself reports for the sample, whatever the size of \(T\). When \(T\) is at or below its degrees of freedom, lavaan reports an RMSEA of 0, from which ci_rmsea could rebuild only \(T = df\); the interval formed from \(T\) itself is narrower the smaller \(T\) is, and its upper limit is 0 when \(T\) lies at or below the (1 - conf_level) / 2 quantile of the central chi square, the convention lavaan and sem_fit_measures share. The replications of a model that fits well often have such statistics, so the distinction matters most when the proposed model is close to the true one. The RMSEA summaries are those of the RMSEA lavaan reports.

The width of the interval depends on the sample size only through \(a\), and ss_aipe_rmsea plans with \(a = N - 1\), the convention of Kelley and Lai (2011). The simulated samples have the planner's necessary_N cases, the size a study would collect, so under lavaan's default \(a = N\) each realized interval is the one lavaan reports for a sample of that size, whose multiplier is one larger than the plan's, and the realized widths sit below the planned width by an amount of order \(1/N\).

The RMSEA is conventionally reported with a 90 percent interval, because a \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval decides the one-sided tests of close and not close fit at level \(\alpha\) (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136), and that is the default here, as in ss_aipe_rmsea.

Note

Replications in which lavaan fails to converge, or for which the RMSEA is undefined, are skipped; the number of converged replications is reported as attr(x, "simulation")$returned. A fit whose likelihood has no maximum, an error variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising (see fa_bifactor), is used as it is, at true_cov_matrix and in a replication: its estimates are wherever lavaan's optimizer stopped on that ridge, but the RMSEA is formed from the chi square alone, which is not, since the likelihood levels off along the ridge and the optimizer stops only where its steps no longer gain. Increase G if many replications fail to converge.

The record of the simulation

Every sensitivity function of the package summarizes its replications over one denominator: the replications that produced a confidence interval (for a power sensitivity function, a test). The proportion of intervals that met the width target (pct_ci_less_width), the proportions of intervals that missed the true value, and the summaries of the widths are all taken over those replications. A replication without an interval is in none of these rows. It is counted, and the returned table carries the counts in its attribute simulation, a list read with attr(x, "simulation"):

attempted

the number of replications asked for (G).

returned

the number that produced an interval (a test).

failed

the number that did not (attempted - returned).

denominator

the number of replications the rows named above are taken over, which is returned.

width_target_probability

the proportion of the replications with an interval whose interval met the width target, the value of the pct_ci_less_width row; NA for a function or a call without a width target, and when no replication produced an interval.

width_target_mc_ci

the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) limits for that proportion, at the confidence level of the table. They describe the error of the simulation, which shrinks as G grows, and nothing else.

A function that records more about its run adds elements to the list, and its help page names them. The line "Replications" beneath the printed table gives G, and the three counts when a replication was without an interval. With many replications without an interval the rows describe only the studies in which the interval could be formed, so failed is to be reported beside them.

References

Cudeck, R., & Browne, M. W. (1992). Constructing a covariance matrix that yields a specified minimizer and a specified minimum discrepancy function value. Psychometrika, 57, 357–369. doi:10.1007/BF02295424

Kelley, K., & Lai, K. (2011). Accuracy in parameter estimation for the root mean square error of approximation: Sample size planning for narrow confidence intervals. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46, 1–32. doi:10.1080/00273171.2011.543027

MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Sugawara, H. M. (1996). Power analysis and determination of sample size for covariance structure modeling. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 130–149. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.2.130

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(2), 1–36. doi:10.18637/jss.v048.i02

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# True data generating model: two correlated factors, each measured by
# three standardized indicators. The factor correlation is 0.5 and every
# loading is 0.7. The implied population covariance matrix is assembled
# from the loading matrix, the factor correlation matrix, and the
# residual variances.
Lambda <- matrix(0, 6, 2)
Lambda[1:3, 1] <- 0.7
Lambda[4:6, 2] <- 0.7
Phi   <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2, 2)
true_cov_matrix <- Lambda %*% Phi %*% t(Lambda) + diag(1 - 0.7^2, 6)
dimnames(true_cov_matrix) <- list(paste0("x", 1:6), paste0("x", 1:6))

# Proposed (misspecified) model: a single common factor.
proposed <- "g =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6"

# The proposed model is fit once at a very large N to recover the
# population RMSEA, the sample size is planned so that the expected width
# of the 90 percent interval is 0.05, and a fresh sample of that size is
# drawn and fit on every replication. Notice that true_rmsea is about
# 0.20, since a single factor is a poor description of two-factor data,
# that the realized widths sit close to the target, and that
# pct_ci_less_width is well away from 0 and 1: planning for the expected
# width aims the average width at the target, not the share of intervals
# narrower than it, which is what assurance controls. G = 10 keeps
# the example quick and estimates that share only roughly; a reported
# sensitivity study deserves the default G = 200 or more.
set.seed(113)
ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(width = 0.05, model = proposed,
                          true_cov_matrix = true_cov_matrix, G = 10)
#>  term               value
#>  mean_rmsea         0.205
#>  median_rmsea       0.208
#>  sd_rmsea           0.017
#>  mean_ci_width      0.050
#>  median_ci_width    0.050
#>  sd_ci_width        0.000
#>  pct_ci_less_width  0.700
#>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.000
#>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.000
#>  total_type_I_error 0.000
#>  total_N            493  
#>  df                 9    
#>  true_rmsea         0.204
#>  width              0.050
#>  conf_level         0.900
#> 
#> Replications: 10
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
